title: Complexity is not rarer in continuous systems, only harder to detect

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Complexity is not rarer in continuous systems, only harder to detect

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Complexity is probably not fundamentally rarer in continuous systems than in discrete ones; it was much easier to discover in discrete systems because they can be studied directly by computer experiment without approximation artifacts.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Probably complexity is not in any fundamental sense rarer in continuous systems than in discrete ones. But the point is that discrete systems can typically be investigated in a much more direct way than continuous ones.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “Continuous Versus Discrete Systems” (from p. 167), p. 167. Scope: continuous versus discrete dynamical systems

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-26: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.43

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing computational resources support comparisons for selected matched families and can quantify detection difficulty. They cannot establish fundamental prevalence across the unbounded spaces of continuous and discrete systems.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define matched description-length distributions over discrete and continuous systems, apply common complexity criteria with numerical-error controls, and compare prevalence and detection rates. Existing samples can test selected families and whether discretization impedes detection.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Observed rarity is confounded by search and publication practices.

Numerical approximations can both hide and create complexity.

There is no natural common sampling measure over continuous and discrete systems.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A paired comparison of discrete cellular automata with continuous cellular automata is computable and speaks to one reading of 'not rarer.' The claim is about continuous systems in general and uses 'probably' and 'fundamentally,' which no sampling measure can nail down. Different ways of drawing formulas produce different rates, so the existing computations test a proxy.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare the fraction of complex outcomes in a fully enumerated discrete family with the fraction in an explicitly sampled continuous family, such as continuous cellular automata with a random constant. A much smaller continuous fraction, stable under several samplings, would challenge 'not fundamentally rarer'; similar fractions would support it for those families.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
There is no natural uniform measure on partial differential equations or on continuous rules, and Wolfram notes that sampling them is ill-posed.

Approximation artifacts, which the claim itself emphasizes, bias any continuous sample toward both false complexity and missed complexity.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.4
discriminating power: 0.3
analysis feasibility: 0.4
data adequacy: 0.35
